title: How to Find Your First Remote Job Without Remote Experience
excerpt: “Previous remote experience preferred” doesn’t have to rule you out. How to pick the right roles, show what you can already do, check the details, and explain it in an interview.
bodyHtml:
You find a job that matches your skills, read through the description, and reach a familiar line: “Previous remote experience preferred.”

If you have always worked in an office, shop, restaurant, or classroom, that sentence can make you hesitate. But “preferred” does not automatically mean mandatory. Before ruling yourself out, look at the role’s essential qualifications and consider how your existing experience matches them.

Finding your first remote job starts with choosing suitable roles, showing evidence of your abilities, and preparing to explain how you would work independently and communicate with a team.

Start with the role, not the word “remote”

Begin by deciding what kind of work you want to do. “Remote” describes a working arrangement, while the job title tells you what an employer needs you to accomplish.

Searching for “remote jobs with no experience” can produce a broad mix of results. A more focused approach is to identify one or two roles connected to skills you already have.

These examples can help you explore possible directions:

  • Retail or hospitality → customer support representative. Highlight answering questions, handling complaints, and explaining options.

  • Administration or reception → administrative assistant or scheduling coordinator. Highlight managing calendars, maintaining records, and organizing tasks.

  • Teaching or tutoring → online tutor or learning support assistant. Highlight explaining concepts, planning lessons, and giving feedback.

  • Sales → sales development representative. Highlight following up, understanding customer needs, and keeping accurate records.

  • Writing or community projects → content assistant or community coordinator. Highlight writing clearly, researching, and coordinating communications.

Treat these as possibilities to investigate. Requirements vary by employer, and some positions need additional training, qualifications, or specialist knowledge.

Read several descriptions for your chosen role and note the responsibilities that appear repeatedly. This gives you a practical guide for deciding which experience to emphasize and which skills to develop.

Also distinguish between being new to remote work and being new to a profession. If you already have relevant professional experience, include positions that match your level of responsibility. Changing your working environment does not necessarily mean starting your career again.

If you are entering the workforce for the first time, focus on junior roles, trainee opportunities, and positions that explicitly provide training. School projects, volunteering, and personal projects may give you useful examples to discuss, provided you describe their context accurately.

Make your experience easy to recognize

Your résumé should make your relevant experience easy to recognize. CareerOneStop recommends emphasizing transferable skills that connect to your target job and describing specific responsibilities and accomplishments. Read CareerOneStop’s résumé guidance.

For example, “responsible for customer service” gives an employer limited information. If accurate, you could write:

Answered customer questions by phone and email, recorded follow-up actions, and coordinated with colleagues to resolve outstanding issues.

Other useful examples might show how you managed deadlines, maintained shared records, learned unfamiliar software, or completed tasks independently.

Include numbers when you have reliable information to support them. If you do not, describe the scope and purpose of your work clearly. Avoid inventing results or presenting an office position as remote employment.

Show it with a small work sample

If your résumé does not clearly demonstrate a relevant skill, consider creating a small work sample. It can illustrate your ability, although it does not replace mandatory qualifications or required experience.

A customer support applicant could write responses to fictional customer questions. An administrative applicant could prepare a sample meeting agenda and weekly schedule. Someone pursuing a content role could create a short editorial calendar and two original posts.

Choose a project that closely resembles a responsibility in your target role. Explain what you created, who it is intended to help, and the reasoning behind your choices. Label practice projects clearly and use fictional or public information.

CareerOneStop identifies work samples as a way to demonstrate skills and the quality of your work. A simple, organized document or PDF can serve this purpose; the presentation should make the sample easy to understand. Read its portfolio guidance.

Use the project to practice relevant tools, too. Look at the software mentioned in job descriptions and focus on useful actions: sharing a document, updating a task, organizing a spreadsheet, or joining a video meeting. Be accurate about your level of familiarity when applying.

Search by role and check the details

Once your materials are ready, search using a specific role and your location requirements. Try phrases such as “remote customer support representative” or “remote junior operations assistant,” then use the available filters to narrow the results.

Check company career pages as well as job boards. For example, We Work Remotely’s customer support listings include positions with different geographic requirements. Read the full employer description even when a listing displays a broad location tag.

Before preparing an application, check:

  • Where the employer can hire and where you must live.

  • Whether you can meet the working hours and time-zone requirements.

  • Whether training, office visits, or travel are required.

  • Whether the position is employment or contract work.

  • Which qualifications are essential and which are preferred.

  • Whether there are equipment, internet, or workspace requirements.

These details matter because remote work can still involve a fixed schedule and an approved working location.

Tailor each application

For each suitable opening, make the connection between your experience and the responsibilities clear. Adjust your résumé summary and bring the most relevant examples forward. Use terminology from the job description when it accurately reflects your skills.

If a cover letter is requested, explain why the work interests you and connect one or two responsibilities to something you have done. Your preference for working from home can be part of your motivation, but the application should also show what you can contribute.

You can also tell former colleagues, classmates, and professional contacts what you are looking for. Naming a particular role and describing your relevant experience makes it easier for someone to recognize a suitable opportunity.

In the interview

When you reach an interview, prepare examples that show how you handle responsibility and communication. Think about a time you met a deadline, resolved a problem, asked for clarification, or kept others informed when plans changed.

If asked about your lack of remote experience, acknowledge it directly. Then explain how your existing habits would help you: organizing priorities, recording progress, communicating clearly, and raising problems early. Support your answer with an example from work, education, volunteering, or a project.

Ask about the employer’s approach as well. How are new employees trained? How does the team communicate priorities? What support is available when someone gets stuck? What would good progress look like during the first month?

Watch for scams

Throughout your search, verify unfamiliar employers and recruiters. The US Federal Trade Commission warns about scams involving payments for promised jobs and fake checks supposedly sent to cover equipment. Do not send money onward from an employer’s check or pay someone for the promise of a job. Read the FTC’s job scam guidance.

Your first week

To get started, set yourself a manageable first-week plan:

  1. Choose one or two target roles and review their requirements.

  2. Update your résumé with relevant, truthful examples.

  3. Prepare a work sample if it would help demonstrate your abilities.

  4. Identify suitable openings and verify the employer and job details.

  5. Submit tailored applications and keep a record of your progress.

Use that record to review your approach. If applications receive little response, check whether you meet the essential requirements and whether your résumé makes the connection clear. If interviews are the difficult part, practice explaining your experience with specific examples.

Your next step can be small: choose one suitable opening, identify the strongest evidence that you could do the work, and build an application around it.
